title: The First Strife of Princes and the Fall of Jeong Do-jeon
description: An evidence-aware historical narrative on the first strife of princes and the fall of jeong do-jeon, separating the retrospective royal annals from events, political claims and later memory.
sourceStatus: Original editorial history with selective primary chronicle and institutional anchors; interpretive statements are attributed contextually, not presented as independent peer review.

blocks.title: A succession dispute becomes an armed confrontation
paragraphs: The first strife of princes in 1398 grew from disagreement over Taejo's chosen succession and the role of powerful ministers. Queen Sindeok's son Yi Bang-seok had been designated heir, while older sons and their supporters disputed the political order around him. Yi Bang-won had played an important part in the dynasty's establishment and resisted a future in which royal princes might be subordinated to ministerial power.

Retrospective accounts written under later kings provide names and episodes but are also shaped by the outcome. The losing faction could be portrayed as threatening rightful heirs, and the victorious faction as restoring proper order. The historian should distinguish the reported attack and deaths from the moral explanations attached to them. The contest turned on actual control of armed men, palace space and succession authority, not only abstract disagreements about the writings of Jeong Do-jeon.

blocks.title: Jeong Do-jeon's position in the conflict
paragraphs: Jeong Do-jeon was a leading architect of the new monarchy and argued for a political structure in which trained ministers would play a major governing role. His opponents associated this position with efforts to reduce princely military autonomy. Yet his intellectual project cannot be condensed into a claim that he wished to abolish monarchy. He worked through the authority of Taejo and defended a particular configuration of royal and ministerial roles.

His killing in 1398 eliminated a powerful figure whose programs had shaped early administrative arrangements. The victors did not thereby reject everything that had been achieved under the founding coalition. State records, offices and the commitment to Confucian government remained significant. This tension illustrates how political winners can selectively inherit their opponents' institutions while erasing them from the moral narrative of legitimacy.

blocks.title: Armed households and the limits of court procedure
paragraphs: In a monarchy whose adult princes possessed influential followers, a formal designation of heir could not by itself compel obedience. Officers and private armed associates had to decide whom to support during a confrontation. The presence of multiple organized groups made succession a matter of military organization as well as kinship.

The violence revealed a central institutional weakness: the sovereign had not fully monopolized military coercion over his relatives. Arguments about duty and seniority became effective only when backed by forces able to defend claimants. It would be mistaken to interpret this exclusively as timeless palace intrigue. The organization of troops was a fundamental question about whether dynastic government could survive the founder's eventual death.

blocks.title: Deaths and the collapse of the chosen succession
paragraphs: The confrontation resulted in the killing of Jeong Do-jeon and other leading ministers together with royal figures associated with the designated heir. The extent to which each victim had independently chosen a political position is not always visible behind the later narrative. Such bloodshed was more than personal revenge: it dismantled the existing succession settlement.

For Taejo the event damaged the prospect of a smooth transfer to the son his household had selected. His subsequent abdication needs to be understood amid coercion, grief and political pressure, rather than as routine retirement. The monarchy remained, but its membership and hierarchy had been violently renegotiated. Descriptions that celebrate the later strength of Taejong should not reduce the lives lost to mere preliminaries of efficient governance.
blocks.label: Original historical synthesis · source-critical

blocks.title: Jeongjong and a provisional settlement
paragraphs: After Taejo stepped down, Jeongjong became king. The arrangement allowed the dynasty to continue without placing Yi Bang-won immediately on the throne. It did not eliminate competition among royal brothers or the role of armed followers. The court's relocation and personnel choices reflected continuing insecurity.

A monarch reigning under such circumstances faced difficult constraints. Official documents could be issued in the king's name while influential princes exercised decisive pressure over policy. The distinction between the legitimacy of a title and actual capacity to command is especially useful for understanding early Joseon. It also helps explain why the later second strife of princes occurred despite the existence of an apparently settled succession.

blocks.title: The problem of remembered justification
paragraphs: The Taejong Annals' account of Yi Bang-won's early career must be read with awareness that later compilers wrote under a dynasty in which he became an honored ruler and ancestor. Statements emphasizing his foresight or portraying enemies as treacherous are evidence for legitimation as well as possible information about events.

A careful history can recognize the violent sequence without endorsing all later accusations. It can also trace institutional consequences: the elimination of rivals, the strengthening of royal authority and the increasing commitment to restricting independent princely forces. The strife is decisive not because it reveals an inevitable path to the throne, but because it forced Joseon's founders to confront the conflict between family power and a centralized monarchy.
